newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Bonn should raise borrowing before taxes - FDP.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Bonn should raise borrowing before taxes - FDP.

text.p: The German government is considering freezing spending and raising borrowing levels for 1997 in order to plug holes in the budget deficit, Wolfgang Gerhardt, chairman of the centrist Free Democrats (FDP) said on Wednesday.
Gerhardt told German Radio that the FDP was strictly against raising taxes to fill the holes because "that would be poison for the economy."
Gerhardt was confirming a reported in the Berliner Morgenpost newspaper on Wednesday that said the government was planning to raise borrowing for the 1997 budget.

"The coalition has to consider a spending freeze as well as raising the new borrowing," he said. "Higher taxes would be contraproductive for the job market and the economy. No one can be interested in that."

Count Otto Lambsdorff, a former economics minister and leader of the FDP, told the Cologne Express newspaper on Wednesday that he expects the tax revenues for 1997 to be 20 billion marks ($12 billion) less than expected.

"There will be a hole of about 20 billion marks," Lambsdorff said. "A certain shortfall of about eight billion has most likely already been factored in so there will be a hole of about 12 billion marks to fill."

Lambsdorff added: "The FDP will not accept tax increases...The missing money has to be saved in the current budget, if necessary with a spending freeze. A slightly higher increase in borrowing is better than tax increases."

The Morgenpost article quoted coalition sources saying that Finance Minister Theo Waigel was preparing a package of measures to close holes in the budget that have opened that would include, among other steps, raising the borrowing levels.
The measures will also include spending cuts, the sources told the newspaper. But the proposal to increase petrol taxes have been dropped because of resistance from the FDP, the sources said.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition met on Tuesday in Bonn to discuss how best to plug yawning gaps in Germany's 1997 budget as other officials started a three-day session to estimate the tax shortfall.
Opposition officials have said 1997 taxes could be running as much as 20 billion marks ($12 billion) below budget projections, mainly due to high unemployment.
Germany, like other European nations, is under pressure to reduce its government deficit to three percent of total economic output this year, to qualify for European monetary union (EMU).
The federal budget foresees a deficit of 53.4 billion marks for 1997, in line with the EMU goal, but many observers are sceptical it can hit the mark.
Waigel has refused to exclude a spending freeze as a possible remedy, and said the government would decide appropriate measures based on the tax estimate.

Federal, state and central bank officials met with private-sector advisors in a semiannual closed-door conference in the east German town of Schwerin to hammer out hard numbers. Their results are due to be announced on Thursday.
On another front, the government on Wednesday said an early sale of part of the state's two-thirds stake in telecommunications giant Deutsche Telekom AG could be on the cards.
"It would be worth considering whether the state should move faster to get rid of its holdings," a spokeswoman for the Finance Ministry in Bonn told Reuters.

She stressed, however, that should the government sell its shares, it would be sure to avoid doing so in a way that could damage either the financial situation of the company or the interests of existing shareholders.
